question.text: What percentage of the vote will the Massachusetts initiative to repeal recreational marijuana legalization receive?
question.resolution_criteria: This question resolves as the percentage of valid votes for yes for [Massachusetts Question 8, Eliminate Recreational Marijuana Sales and Allow Limited Possession Initiative (2026)](https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_8,_Eliminate_Recreational_Marijuana_Sales_and_Allow_Limited_Possession_Initiative_(2026)), rounded to the nearest percentage point.

# Massachusetts Question 8 (2026), recreational marijuana repeal: research brief

## 1. Resolution source
- 2026-10-24: I tried to fetch the Ballotpedia page for Question 8, but the content came back empty, so I could not see what it currently shows. No results are expected there until after the November 3 election. [Ballotpedia](https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_8,_Eliminate_Recreational_Marijuana_Sales_and_Allow_Limited_Possession_Initiative_(2026))
- What the measure does: it would end licensed adult-use retail sales, distribution and taxation and ban home growing for non-medical use. Medical sales and limited possession would stay legal. [WBUR](https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/09/massachusetts-ballot-question-8-cannabis-weed-pot-repeal), [Boston Herald](https://www.bostonherald.com/2026/10/23/editorial-question-8-takes-wrong-approach-to-weed-problems/)

## 2. Current status
- Nothing has settled the question yet. The election is 2026-11-03, and early in-person voting runs through 2026-10-30. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day count if they arrive by 2026-11-06 at 5 PM. [Jamaica Plain Gazette](http://jamaicaplaingazette.com/2026/10/23/early-voting-is-underway/)
- Every public poll shows Yes trailing badly, with support between 21% and 33%.

## 3. Recent news (newest first)
- 2026-10-23: The Boston Herald editorial board urges a No vote. [Boston Herald](https://www.bostonherald.com/2026/10/23/editorial-question-8-takes-wrong-approach-to-weed-problems/)
- 2026-10-23: JD Supra's "The Week in Weed" says the repeal is "losing badly in polls." [JD Supra](https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/the-week-in-weed-october-2026-3-9947734/)
- 2026-10-22: More than 50 state lawmakers oppose the measure, including House Speaker Mariano and Senate President Spilka. Senators Warren and Markey, Gov. Healey, Rep. Pressley and Boston Mayor Wu have also said they will vote No. [NORML](https://norml.org/news/2026/10/22/massachusetts-lawmakers-urge-no-vote-on-marijuana-repeal-effort-question-8-latest-poll-shows-little-public-support)
- 2026-10-20: Suffolk/Boston Globe poll, fielded Oct 14-17/18 with 500 likely voters (±4.4): Yes 21%, No 71%, undecided 7%. [Marijuana Herald](https://themarijuanaherald.com/2026/10/massachusetts-21-question-8/), [Yahoo](https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/massachusetts-voters-oppose-marijuana-legalization-194541510.html)
- 2026-10-19: UMass Amherst/WCVB poll, fielded Oct 5-12 with 852 registered voters (±4.2): Yes 31%, No 61% (47% definitely, 14% probably), undecided 5%, did not understand 3%. Support for repeal is 44% among Republicans and 41% among non-users. Question 8 has the lowest support of the nine statewide questions. [Yahoo](https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/massachusetts-voters-oppose-marijuana-legalization-194541510.html), [MJBizDaily](https://mjbizdaily.com/news/latest-poll-shows-massachusetts-adult-use-cannabis-sales-repeal-failing-badly/618736/)
- October 2026: The Yes side, the Coalition for a Healthy Massachusetts, is running ads on impaired driving. The No on 8 campaign has put out its own ads. [Marijuana Moment](https://www.marijuanamoment.net/massachusetts-anti-marijuana-ballot-campaign-launches-new-ads-focused-on-impaired-driving/), [Marijuana Moment](https://www.marijuanamoment.net/new-ads-urge-massachusetts-voters-to-keep-marijuana-sales-legal-by-rejecting-measure-on-november-ballot/)
- Money: Wikipedia says supporters have spent more than $3.6M, almost all from Smart Approaches to Marijuana (SAM Action, based in Virginia), and opponents about $1.5M, mostly from the state's cannabis businesses. I did not check these figures against the state campaign finance office. Other reports put SAM's money at about $3.0M to $3.5M. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Massachusetts_ballot_measures), [Cannabis Business Times](https://www.cannabisbusinesstimes.com/us-states/massachusetts/news/15834274/sam-contributes-32-million-in-dark-money-to-massachusetts-cannabis-prohibition-campaign), [MJBizDaily](https://mjbizdaily.com/?p=617991)

## 4. Base rates
All Question 8 polls, as listed on Wikipedia ([source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Massachusetts_ballot_measures)):

| Field dates | Pollster | Sample | Yes | No | Undecided |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Aug 5-12 | UMass/WCVB | registered voters | 33% | 55% | 10% |
| Sep 14-22 | MassINC/CommonWealth Beacon | likely voters | 27% | 61% | 12% |
| Sep 17-21 | UNH | likely voters | 24% | 71% | 5% |
| Oct 5-12 | UMass/WCVB | registered voters | 31% | 61% | 8% |
| Oct 14-18 | Suffolk/Globe | likely voters | 21% | 71% | 7% |

- The five-poll average is about 27% Yes. The two-way Yes share works out to roughly 23% to 36%, about 30% on average.
- Trend: the UMass series went from 33% to 31% Yes while No rose from 55% to 61%. Likely-voter polls show lower Yes numbers than registered-voter polls.
- 2016 comparison: Question 4, which legalized recreational marijuana, passed 53.7% to 46.3%. So about 46% opposed legalization before it took effect. This is from my background knowledge; I did not fetch a page this session ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Massachusetts_Question_4)).
- General pattern (also background knowledge, not checked this session): undecided voters on ballot measures tend to break toward No, and Yes shares often fall between polling and Election Day. This measure has never been tested before; it is the first public vote on repealing an existing adult-use law. [NORML](https://norml.org/news/2026/10/22/massachusetts-lawmakers-urge-no-vote-on-marijuana-repeal-effort-question-8-latest-poll-shows-little-public-support)

## 5. Other forecasts
- 2026-10-24: Kalshi, "Which ballot measures will pass in Massachusetts?": Question 8 trades at 4% Yes, meaning 4% implied odds of passing. This is about passing, not the vote share. (Prices were collected by code before this session; I did not open the market.)
- Related Kalshi markets suggest a strongly Democratic electorate: Healey at least 60% trades around 48%, and Markey at least 62% around 56%.
- I could not find any Polymarket, Manifold or Metaculus market on Question 8's vote share, or any expert vote-share forecast.

## 6. Upcoming events before resolution
- 2026-10-27, 5 PM: deadline for mail ballots to be received by local offices. [JP Gazette](http://jamaicaplaingazette.com/2026/10/23/early-voting-is-underway/)
- 2026-10-30: early in-person voting ends.
- More polls are possible in the final week, for example new MassINC, UNH or Emerson releases. None found as of 2026-10-24.
- Late spending: SAM's money advantage of about 2 to 1 could pay for a final ad push.
- 2026-11-03: Election Day. Mail ballots arriving by 2026-11-06 still count, so the vote share may shift slightly as late ballots are counted. Certification comes after that.

forecasts.reasoning:
(a) About 10 days remain until the November 3, 2026 election. Late mail ballots count through November 6, and the question resolves around November 10.

(b) The resolution source has no results yet. The latest polls are Suffolk/Globe (Oct 14-18, likely voters), with Yes 21% and No 71%, and UMass/WCVB (Oct 5-12, registered voters), with Yes 31% and No 61%.

(c) If nothing changed, the five-poll average of about 27% Yes would carry forward. Allocating undecided voters gives a two-way Yes share of about 29-30%.

(d) The trend is flat to slightly worse for Yes. UMass moved from 33% to 31%, No has risen across pollsters, and likely-voter polls show lower Yes numbers. Continuing that trend points to about 26-29% Yes.

(e) Final results for ballot measures often differ from late polls by 3-7 points, sometimes more. Uncommon measures that poll in the low 20s often end up a few points higher, because there is a floor of social-conservative and older voters. In 2016, 46% opposed legalization. Republicans currently support repeal at about 44%, and Trump took about 36% in Massachusetts in 2024. Both suggest Yes is unlikely to drop below the low 20s.

(f) Kalshi gives the measure a 4% chance of passing, which is consistent with a Yes share in the 20s to mid-30s. Nearly all political figures and editorial boards oppose it. The Yes side has outspent the No side by roughly 2 to 1.

(g) Low scenario: high Democratic turnout and undecideds breaking firmly toward No push Yes down to about 20-22%, matching the Suffolk poll. High scenario: SAM's late ad push on impaired driving, confused voting on "Yes," and a polling miss among older and conservative voters lift Yes to the high 30s or around 40%.

(a) About 10 days until the November 3, 2026 election. Results should be clear by November 4, and certified figures will follow before about November 10.

(b) Ballotpedia has no results yet. The latest data are polls. Suffolk/Globe (Oct 14-18, likely voters) has Yes 21%, No 71%. UMass/WCVB (Oct 5-12, registered voters) has Yes 31%, No 61%.

(c) If nothing changed, the polls put Yes at about 30% once undecideds are split proportionally. The five polls give two-way Yes shares of roughly 36, 34, 31, 25 and 23 (Aug to Oct).

(d) If the trend continued, Yes would drift slightly lower. The Yes share has drifted down and No has grown, and likely-voter polls show lower Yes numbers. That points to roughly 26-29%.

(e) Historical variation: final results on marijuana measures typically land within about 3-6 points of the poll average.
- 2016 Massachusetts Q4: polls overstated legalization support somewhat, and it passed 53.7% to 46.3%.
- Polls sometimes understate anti-marijuana sentiment, plausibly because of a social desirability effect. That could lift Yes a bit above the polls.
- Undecideds and status quo bias usually favor No.

(f) Markets and experts:
- Kalshi gives Question 8 about a 4% chance of passing, which fits a Yes share well below 50%.
- Media and the measure's opponents describe it as "losing badly."
- The electorate looks strongly Democratic: Healey's vote share is trading around 60%.
- There is no market on the vote share itself.

(g) Unexpected scenarios:
- Low: a Democratic-heavy turnout surge plus a late No campaign push collapses Yes to around 20-22%, matching the Suffolk poll.
- High: polls understate repeal support, much as the 2016 polls understated opposition. SAM's late ad blitz on impaired driving and the 46% of voters who opposed legalization in 2016 could push Yes into the high 30s or about 40%.

(a) **Time left:** The election is November 3, 2026, about 10 days away. Late mail ballots count through November 6, and the question resolves around November 10.

(b) **Latest known value:** There are no results yet. The latest polls are:
- Suffolk/Globe, October 14-18, likely voters: Yes 21%, No 71%.

The five-poll average is about 27% Yes, or about 30% once undecided voters are set aside.

(c) **If nothing changed:** Splitting undecided voters in proportion to the decided ones gives roughly 23% to 34% Yes. The midpoint is about 29% to 30%.

(d) **If the current trend continued:** The No side is gaining slowly, and likely-voter polls show lower Yes numbers. Taken alone, that points to Yes in the mid-to-high 20s.

(e) **Historical variation:** Polls on lopsided ballot measures often miss the final Yes share by 5 to 10 points. Losing measures in Massachusetts tend to land above 30%:
- 2024 Question 4 (psychedelics) got about 43%.
- 2024 Question 5 (tipped wages) got about 36%.

There is also a structural floor. Republicans, who make up about a third of the electorate based on Deaton's roughly 34%, back repeal at about 44%. In 2016, 46% voted against legalizing.

(f) **Experts and markets:** Kalshi gives Question 8 a 4% chance of passing, which fits a Yes share of about 25% to 38%. I found no market on the vote share itself.

(g) **Unexpected scenarios:**
- **Low outcome:** Turnout is heavily Democratic and young, SAM's ads fall flat, and the Suffolk poll proves accurate, leaving Yes at about 20% to 23%.
- **High outcome:** Voters are reluctant to tell pollsters they support repeal, the impaired-driving ads persuade older suburban voters, and some voters misread what a Yes vote does, pushing Yes to about 38% to 42%.

(a) About 10 days remain until the November 3, 2026 election. Results should be clear by election night or within a few days, with resolution around November 10.

(b) The resolution source, Ballotpedia, will have no results until after November 3. The latest polling data point is the Suffolk/Globe poll from October 14-18: Yes 21%, No 71%, undecided 7%. That is about 23% Yes when undecideds are excluded.

(c) If nothing changed, the polls would hold. The five-poll average of the two-way Yes share is about 30%, with individual polls ranging from roughly 23% to 36%.

(d) If the trend continued, Yes would edge slightly lower. No has been gaining in the UMass series and in likely-voter polls, and undecided voters on ballot measures usually break toward No. That points to about 26-30%.

(e) Historical variation: polling error on marijuana ballot measures is often 5 points or more. Polls have tended to overstate the pro-cannabis side:
- Florida 2024 polled at 60% or more and passed with 56%.
- Several 2022 legalization measures in Arkansas and the Dakotas underperformed their polls.

A "shy prohibitionist" effect could therefore lift the Yes share here. Massachusetts voters opposed legalization by about 46% in 2016, which shows a real anti-cannabis base, although the state has grown more accepting since then.

(f) Expert and market expectations:
- Kalshi gives the measure about a 4% chance of passing, which is consistent with a vote share in the high 20s to mid 30s.
- No vote-share market or expert forecast exists.
- The Yes side has spent about twice as much as the No side.

(g) Unexpected scenarios:
- Low outcome: a heavily Democratic, high-turnout electorate, together with opposition from the major endorsers (Healey, Warren, Markey, Wu), pushes Yes down to around 22%.
- High outcome: a late impaired-driving ad blitz from SAM, polls that understate older and suburban voters, and confusion over the "allow limited possession" wording push Yes to around 40%.

My median is about 31%. That allows for a modest upward adjustment from the polls, because marijuana-measure polls have historically understated the anti-cannabis side, and it is offset by undecided voters breaking toward No.
